You may make a crab-stock to become a good tree, by grafting into it a shoot from a good tree, and then the fruit will be good; but if the tree be still the same, plant it where you will, and water it how you will, the fruit will be still corrupt." Note, Unless the heart be <hi type="italic">trans</hi>formed, the life will never be thoroughly <hi type="italic">re</hi>formed. These Pharisees were shy of speaking out their wicked thoughts of Jesus Christ; but Christ here intimates, how vain it was for them to seek to hide that root of bitterness in them, that bore this gall and wormwood, when they never sought to mortify it. Note, It should be more our care to be good really, than to seem good outwardly. <div eID="gen22216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22217" type="x-p"/> (2.) The heart is the <hi type="italic">fountain,</hi> the words are the streams (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.34">v. 34</reference>); <hi type="italic">Out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks,</hi> as the streams are the overflowings of the spring. A wicked heart is said to <hi type="italic">send forth wickedness, as a fountain casts forth her waters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.6.7">Jer. vi. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">A troubled fountain, and a corrupt spring,</hi> such as Solomon speaks of (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.26">Prov. xxv. 26</reference>), must needs <hi type="italic">send forth muddy and unpleasant streams.</hi> Evil words are the natural, genuine product of an evil heart. Nothing but the salt of grace, cast into the spring, will heal the waters, <hi type="italic">season the speech,</hi> and purify the <hi type="italic">corrupt communications.</hi> This they wanted, they were evil; <hi type="italic">and how can ye, being evil, speak good things?</hi> They were <hi type="italic">a generation of vipers;</hi> John Baptist had called them so (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.7">ch. iii. 7</reference>), and they were still the same; for <hi type="italic">can the Ethiopian change his skin?</hi> The people looked upon the Pharisees as a generation of saints, but Christ calls them <hi type="italic">a generation of vipers, the seed of the serpent,</hi> that had an enmity to Christ and his gospel. Now what could be expected from <hi type="italic">a generation of vipers,</hi> but that which is poisonous and malignant? Can the viper be otherwise than venomous? Note, Bad things may be expected from bad people, as said the proverb of the ancients, <hi type="italic">Wickedness proceedeth from the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.13">1 Sam. xxiv. 13</reference>. <hi type="italic">The vile person will speak villany,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.6">Isa. xxxii. 6</reference>. Those who are themselves evil, have neither skill nor will to speak good things, as they should be spoken. Christ would have his disciples know what sort of men they were to live among, that they might know what to look for. They are as Ezekiel <hi type="italic">among scorpions</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.2.6">Ezek. ii. 6</reference>), and must not think it strange if they be stung and bitten. <div eID="gen22217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22218" type="x-p"/> (3.) The heart is the <hi type="italic">treasury,</hi> the words are the things brought out of that treasury (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.35">v. 35</reference>); and from hence men's characters may be drawn, and may be judged of. <div eID="gen22218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22219" type="x-p"/> [1.] It is the character of a <hi type="italic">good man,</hi> that he has a <hi type="italic">good treasure in his heart,</hi> and from thence <hi type="italic">brings forth good things,</hi> as there is occasion. Graces, comforts, experiences, good knowledge, good affections, good resolutions, these are a <hi type="italic">good treasure in the heart;</hi> the word of God hidden there, the law of God written there, divine truths dwelling and ruling thee, are a treasure there, valuable and suitable, kept safe and kept secret, as the stores of the good householder, but ready for use upon all occasions. <hi type="italic">A good man,</hi> thus furnished, will <hi type="italic">bring forth,</hi> as Joseph out of his stores; will be speaking and doing that which is good, for God's glory, and the edification of others. See <reference osisRef="Prov.10.11 Prov.10.13 Prov.10.14 Prov.10.20 Prov.10.21 Prov.10.31 Prov.10.32">Prov. x. 11, 13, 14, 20, 21, 31, 32</reference>. This is <hi type="italic">bringing forth good things.</hi> Some pretend to good expenses that have not a <hi type="italic">good treasure</hi>—such will soon be bankrupts: some pretend to have a good treasure within, but give no proof of it: they hope they have it in them, and thank God, whatever their words and actions are, they have good hearts; but <hi type="italic">faith without works is dead:</hi> and some have a <hi type="italic">good treasure</hi> of wisdom and knowledge, but they are not communicative, they do not <hi type="italic">bring forth</hi> out of it: they have a talent, but know not how to trade with it. The complete Christian in <hi type="italic">this</hi> bears the image of God, that he both <hi type="italic">is good, and does good.</hi> <div eID="gen22219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22220" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is the character of <hi type="italic">an evil man,</hi> that he has an <hi type="italic">evil treasure in his heart,</hi> and out of it <hi type="italic">bringeth forth evil things.</hi> Lusts and corruptions dwelling and reigning in the heart are an evil treasure, out of which the sinner brings forth bad words and actions, to the dishonour of God, and the hurt of others. See <reference osisRef="Gen.6.5 Gen.6.12 Matt.15.18-Matt.15.20">Gen. vi. 5, 12; Matt. xv. 18-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.1.15">Jam. i. 15</reference>. But <hi type="italic">treasures of wickedness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.2">Prov. x. 2</reference>) will be <hi type="italic">treasures of wrath.</hi> <div eID="gen22220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22221" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ speaks here concerning <hi type="italic">idle words,</hi> and shows what evil there is in them (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.36-Matt.12.37">v. 36, 37</reference>); much more is there in such wicked words as the Pharisees spoke. It concerns us to think much of the day of judgment, that <hi type="italic">that</hi> may be a check upon our tongues; and let us consider, <div eID="gen22221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22222" type="x-p"/> (1.) How particular the account will be of tongue-sins in that day: even <hi type="italic">for every idle words,</hi> or discourse, <hi type="italic">that men speak, they shall give account.</hi> This intimates, [1.] That God takes notice of every word we say, even that which we ourselves do not notice. See <reference osisRef="Ps.139.4">Psalm cxxxix. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Not a word in my tongue but thou knowest it:</hi> though spoken without regard or design, God takes cognizance of it. [2.] That vain, idle, impertinent talk is displeasing to God, which tends not to any good purpose, is not good to any use of edifying; it is the product of a vain and trifling heart. These <hi type="italic">idle words</hi> are the same with that <hi type="italic">foolish talking and jesting</hi> which is forbidden, <reference osisRef="Eph.5.4">Eph. v. 4</reference>. This is that sin which is seldom wanting in <hi type="italic">the multitude of words, unprofitable talk,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.15.3">Job xv. 3</reference>. [3.] We must shortly account for these idle words; they will be produced in evidence against us, to prove us unprofitable servants, that have not improved the faculties of reason and speech, which are part of the talents we are entrusted with. If we repent not of our idle words, and our account for them be not balanced by the blood of Christ, we are undone. <div eID="gen22222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22223" type="x-p"/> (2.) How strict the judgment will be upon that account (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.37">v. 37</reference>); <hi type="italic">By thy words thou shall be justified or condemned;</hi> a common rule in men's judgments, and here applied to God's. Note, The constant tenour of our discourse, according as it is gracious or not gracious, will be an evidence for us, or against us, at the great day. Those who seemed to be religious, but bridled not their tongue, will then be found to have put a cheat upon themselves with a vain religion, <reference osisRef="Jas.1.26">Jam. i. 26</reference>. Some think that Christ here refers to that of Eliphaz (<reference osisRef="Job.15.6">Job xv. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thine own mouth condemneth thee, and not I;</hi> or, rather, to that of Solomon (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.21">Prov. xviii. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">Death and life are in the power of the tongue.</hi>
entries.e06d032b352dd1b5c818b38bffca86c30b694e76: <div eID="gen22223" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Pharisees Ask a Sign.</title> <div sID="gen22224" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">38</hi> Then certain of the scribes and of the Pharisees answered, saying, Master, we would see a sign from thee. 39 But he answered and said unto them, An evil and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas: <hi type="super">40</hi> For as Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly; so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth. <hi type="super">41</hi> The men of Nineveh shall rise in judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: because they repented at the preaching of Jonas; and, behold, a greater than Jonas <hi type="italic">is</hi> here. <hi type="super">42</hi> The queen of the south shall rise up in the judgment with this generation, and shall condemn it: for she came from the uttermost parts of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon; and, behold, a greater than Solomon <hi type="italic">is</hi> here. <hi type="super">43</hi> When the unclean spirit is gone out of a man, he walketh through dry places, seeking rest, and findeth none. <hi type="super">44</hi> Then he saith, I will return into my house from whence I came out; and when he is come, he findeth <hi type="italic">it</hi> empty, swept, and garnished. 45 Then goeth he, and taketh with himself seven other spirits more wicked than himself, and they enter in and dwell there: and the last <hi type="italic">state</hi> of that man is worse than the first. Even so shall it be also unto this wicked generation. <div eID="gen22224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22225" type="x-p"/> It is probable that these Pharisees with whom Christ is here in discourse were not the same that cavilled at him (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.24">v. 24</reference>), and would not credit the signs he gave; but another set of them, who saw that there was no reason to discredit them, but would not content themselves with the signs he gave, nor admit the evidence of them, unless he would give them such further proof as they should demand. Here is, <div eID="gen22225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22226" type="x-p"/> I. Their address to him, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.38">v. 38</reference>. They compliment him with the title of <hi type="italic">Master,</hi> pretending respect for him, when they intended to abuse him; all are not indeed Christ's servants, who call him <hi type="italic">Master.</hi> Their request is, <hi type="italic">We would see a sign from thee.</hi> It was highly reasonable that they should see a sign, that he should by miracles prove his divine mission: see <reference osisRef="Exod.4.8-Exod.4.9">Exod. iv. 8, 9</reference>. He came to take down a model of religion that was set up by miracles, and therefore it was requisite he should produce the same credentials; but it was highly unreasonable to demand a sign now, when he had given so many signs already, that did abundantly prove him <hi type="italic">sent of God.</hi> Note, It is natural to proud men to <hi type="italic">pre</hi>scribe to God, and then to make that an excuse for not <hi type="italic">sub</hi>scribing to him; but a man's <hi type="italic">of</hi>fence will never be his <hi type="italic">de</hi>fence. <div eID="gen22226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22227" type="x-p"/> II. His answer to this address, this insolent demand, <div eID="gen22227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22228" type="x-p"/> 1. He condemns the demand, as the language of <hi type="italic">an evil and adulterous generation,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.12.39">v. 39</reference>. He fastens the charge, not only on <hi type="italic">the scribes and Pharisees,</hi> but the whole nation of the Jews; they were all like their leaders, a seed and succession of evil-doers: they were an evil generation indeed, that not only hardened themselves against the conviction of Christ's miracles, but set themselves to abuse him, and put contempt on his miracles. They were <hi type="italic">an adulterous generation,</hi> (1.) As an adulterous brood; so miserably degenerated from the faith and obedience of their ancestors, that Abraham and Israel acknowledged them not. See <reference osisRef="Isa.57.3">Isa. lvii. 3</reference>. Or, (2.) As an adulterous wife; they departed from that God, to whom by covenant they had been espoused: they were not guilty of the whoredom of idolatry, as they had been before the captivity, but they were guilty of infidelity, and all iniquity, and that is whoredom too: they did not look after gods of their own making, but they looked for signs of their own devising; and that was adultery. <div eID="gen22228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22229" type="x-p"/> 2. He refuses to give them any other sign than he has already given them, but <hi type="italic">that of the prophet Jonas.</hi> Note, Though Christ is always ready to hear and answer holy desires and prayers, yet he will not gratify corrupt lusts and humours. Those who <hi type="italic">ask amiss, ask, and have not.</hi> Signs were granted to those who desired them for the confirmation of their faith, as to Abraham and Gideon; but were denied to those who demanded them for the excuse of their unbelief. <div eID="gen22229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22230" type="x-p"/> Justly might Christ have said, They shall never see another miracle: but see his wonderful goodness; (1.) They shall have the same signs still repeated, for their further benefit, and more abundant conviction. (2.) They shall have one sign of a different kind from all these, and that is, <hi type="italic">the resurrection of Christ from the dead by his own power,</hi> called here <hi type="italic">the sign of the prophet Jonas</hi> this was yet reserved for their conviction, and was intended to be the great proof of Christ's being the Messiah; for by that he was <hi type="italic">declared to be the Son of God with power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.4">Rom. i. 4</reference>. That was such a sign as surpassed all the rest, completed and crowned them. "<hi type="italic">If they will not believe</hi> the former signs, they will believe this (<reference osisRef="Exod.4.9">Exod. iv. 9</reference>), and if this will not convince them, nothing will." And yet the unbelief of the Jews found out an evasion to shift off that too, by saying, <hi type="italic">His disciples came and stole him away;</hi> for none are so incurably blind as those who are resolved they will not see. <div eID="gen22230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22231" type="x-p"/> Now this sign of the prophet Jonas he further explains here; (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.40">v. 40</reference>) <hi type="italic">As Jonas was three days and three nights in the whale's belly,</hi> and then came out again safe and well, thus Christ shall be so long in the grave, and then shall rise again. [1.] The grave was to Christ as the belly of the fish was to Jonah; thither he was thrown, as a Ransom for lives ready to be lost in a storm; there he lay, as <hi type="italic">in the belly of hell</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.2">Jonah ii. 2</reference>), and seemed to be cast out of God's sight. [2.] He continued in the grave just as long as Jonah continued in the fish's belly, <hi type="italic">three days and three nights;</hi> not three whole days and nights: it is probable, Jonah did not lie so long in the whale's belly, but part of three natural days (<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">nychthemerai</hi></hi>, the Greeks called them); he was buried in the afternoon of the sixth day of the week, and rose again in the morning of the first day; it is a manner of speech very usual; see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.29">1 Kings xx. 29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.4.16">Esth. iv. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.5.1">v. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.21">Luke ii. 21</reference>. So long Jonah was a prisoner for his own sins, so long Christ was a Prisoner for ours. [3.] As Jonah in the whale's belly comforted himself with an assurance that yet he should look again <hi type="italic">toward God's holy temple</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jonah.2.4">Jonah ii. 4</reference>), so Christ when he lay in the grave, is expressly said to <hi type="italic">rest in hope,</hi> as one assured he should <hi type="italic">not see corruption,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.2.26-Acts.2.27">Acts ii. 26, 27</reference>. [4.] As Jonah on the third day was discharged from his prison, and came to the land of the living again, from <hi type="italic">the congregation of the dead</hi> (for dead things are said to be <hi type="italic">formed from under the waters,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.26.5">Job xxvi. 5</reference>), so Christ on the third day should return to life, and rise out of his grave to send abroad the gospel to the Gentiles. <div eID="gen22231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22232" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ takes this occasion to represent the sad character and condition of that generation in which he lived, a generation that would not be reformed, and therefore could not but be ruined; and he gives them their character, as it would stand in the day of judgment, under the full discoveries and final sentences of that day. Persons and things now appear under false colours; characters and conditions are here changeable: if therefore we would make a right estimate, we must take our measures from the last judgment; things are really, what they are eternally. <div eID="gen22232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22233" type="x-p"/> Now Christ represents the people of the Jews, <div eID="gen22233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22234" type="x-p"/> (1.) As a generation that would be condemned by the <hi type="italic">men of Nineveh,</hi> whose <hi type="italic">repenting at the preaching of Jonas</hi> would <hi type="italic">rise up in judgment</hi> against them, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.41">v. 41</reference>. Christ's resurrection will be the sign of the prophet Jonas to them: but it will not have so happy an effect upon them, as that of Jonas had upon the Ninevites, for they were by it brought to such a repentance as prevented their ruin; but the Jews will be hardened in an unbelief that shall hasten their ruin; and in the day of judgment, the repentance of the Ninevites will be mentioned as an aggravation of the sin, and consequently the condemnation of those to whom Christ preached then, and of those to whom Christ is preached now; for this reason, because Christ is greater than Jonah. [1.] Jonah was but a man, subject to like passions, to like sinful passions, as we are; but Christ is the Son of God. [2.] Jonah was a stranger in Nineveh, he came among the strangers that were prejudiced against his country; but Christ came to his own, when he preached to the Jews, and much more when he is preached among professing Christians, that are called by his name. [3.] Jonah preached but one short sermon, and that with no great solemnity, but as he passed along the streets; Christ renews his calls, sat and taught, taught in the synagogues. [4.] Jonah preached nothing but wrath and ruin within forty days, gave no instructions, directions, or encouragements, to repent: but Christ, besides the warning given us of our danger, has shown wherein we must repent, and assured us of acceptance upon our repentance, because <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven is at hand.</hi> [5.] Jonah wrought no miracle to confirm his doctrine, showed no good will to the Ninevites; but Christ wrought abundance of miracles, and all miracles of mercy: yet the Ninevites <hi type="italic">repented at the preaching of Jonas,</hi> but the Jews were not wrought upon by Christ's preaching. Note, The goodness of some, who have less helps and advantages for their souls, will aggravate the badness of those who have much greater. Those who by the twilight discover <hi type="italic">the things that belong to their peace,</hi> will shame those who grope at noon-day. <div eID="gen22234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22235" type="x-p"/> (2.) As a generation that would be condemned by the queen of the south, the queen of Sheba, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.42">v. 42</reference>. The Ninevites would shame them for not repenting, the queen of Sheba for not believing in Christ. She came from a far country to hear the wisdom of Solomon; yet people will not be persuaded to come and hear the wisdom of Christ, though he is in every thing greater than Solomon. [1.] The queen of Sheba had no invitation to come to Solomon, nor any promise of being welcome; but we are invited to Christ, to sit at his feet and hear his word. [2.] Solomon was but a wise man, but Christ is wisdom itself, <hi type="italic">in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom.</hi> [3.] The queen of Sheba had many difficulties to break through; she was a woman, unfit for travel, the journey long and perilous; she was a queen, and what would become of her own country in her absence? We have no such cares to hinder us. [4.] She could not be sure that it would be worth her while to go so far on this errand; fame uses to flatter men, and perhaps she might have in her own country or court wise men sufficient to instruct her; yet, having heard of Solomon's fame, she would see him; but we come not to Christ upon such uncertainties. [5.] <hi type="italic">She came from the uttermost parts of the earth,</hi> but we have Christ among us, and his word nigh us: <hi type="italic">Behold he stands at the door, and knocks.</hi> [6.] It should seem the wisdom the queen of Sheba came for was only philosophy and politics; but the wisdom that is to be had with Christ is wisdom to salvation. [7.] She could only <hi type="italic">hear</hi> Solomon's wisdom; he could not <hi type="italic">give</hi> her wisdom: but Christ will give wisdom to those who come to him; nay, he will himself be <hi type="italic">made of God to them Wisdom;</hi> so that, upon all these accounts, if we do not hear the wisdom of Christ, the forwardness of the queen of Sheba to come and hear the wisdom of Solomon will rise up in judgment against us and condemn us; for Jesus Christ is greater than Solomon. <div eID="gen22235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22236" type="x-p"/> (3.) As a generation that were resolved to continue in the possession, and under the power, of Satan, notwithstanding all the methods that were used to dispossess him and rescue them. They are compared to one out of whom the devil is gone, but returns with double force, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.43-Matt.12.45">v. 43-45</reference>. The devil is here called <hi type="italic">the unclean spirit,</hi> for he has lost all his purity, and delights in and promotes all manner of impurity among men. Now, <div eID="gen22236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22237" type="x-p"/> [1.] The parable represents his possessing men's bodies: Christ having lately cast out a devil, and they having said <hi type="italic">he had a devil,</hi> gave occasion to show how much they were under the power of Satan. This is a further proof that Christ did not cast out devils by compact with the devil, for then he would soon have returned again; but Christ's ejectment of him was final, and such as barred a re-entry: we find him charging the evil spirit to <hi type="italic">go out, and enter no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.9.25">Mark ix. 25</reference>. Probably the devil was wont sometimes thus to sport with those he had possession of; he would go out, and then return again with more fury; hence the lucid intervals of those in that condition were commonly followed with the more violent fits. When the devil is gone out, he is uneasy, for <hi type="italic">he sleeps not except he have done mischief</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.16">Prov. iv. 16</reference>); <hi type="italic">he walks in dry places,</hi> like one that is very melancholy; he <hi type="italic">seeks rest but finds none,</hi> till he returns again. When Christ cast the legion out of the man, they begged leave to enter into the swine, where they went not long in dry places, but into the lake presently. <div eID="gen22237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22238" type="x-p"/> [2.] The application of the parable makes it to represent the case of the body of the Jewish church and nation: <hi type="italic">So shall it be with this wicked generation,</hi> that now resist, and will finally reject, the gospel of Christ. The devil, who by the labours of Christ and his disciples had been cast out of many of the Jews, sought for rest among the heathen, from whose persons and temples the Christians would every where expel him: so Dr. Whitby: or finding no where else in the heathen world such pleasant, desirable habitations, to his satisfaction, as here in the heart of the Jews: so Dr. Hammond: he shall therefore enter again into them, for Christ had not found admission among them, and they, by their prodigious wickedness and obstinate unbelief, were still more ready than ever to receive him; and then he shall take a durable possession here, and the state of this people is likely to be more desperately damnable (so Dr. Hammond) than it was before Christ came among them, or would have been if Satan had never been cast out. <div eID="gen22238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22239" type="x-p"/> The body of that nation is here represented, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> As an apostate people. After the captivity in Babylon, they began to reform, left their idols, and appeared with some face of religion; but they soon corrupted themselves again: though they never relapsed into idolatry, they fell into all manner of impiety and profaneness, grew worse and worse, and added to all the rest of their wickedness a wilful contempt of, and opposition to, Christ and his gospel. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> As a people marked for ruin. A new commission was passing the seals against that hypocritical nation, the people of God's wrath (like that, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.6">Isa. x. 6</reference>), and their destruction by the Romans was likely to be greater than any other, as their sins had been more flagrant: then it was <hi type="italic">that wrath came upon them to the uttermost,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.15-1Thess.2.16">1 Thess. ii. 15, 16</reference>. Let this be a warning to all nations and churches, to take heed of leaving their first love, of letting fall a good work of reformation begun among them, and returning to that wickedness which they seemed to have forsaken; <hi type="italic">for the last state of such will be worse than the first.</hi>
entries.f7d61b9ca903543f60708de2baea27e40fe13ae3: <div eID="gen22239" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Who Are Christ's Relations.</title> <div sID="gen22240" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">46</hi> While he yet talked to the people, behold, <hi type="italic">his</hi> mother and his brethren stood without, desiring to speak with him. <hi type="super">47</hi> Then one said unto him, Behold, thy mother and thy brethren stand without, desiring to speak with thee. <hi type="super">48</hi> But he answered and said unto him that told him, Who is my mother? and who are my brethren? <hi type="super">49</hi> And he stretched forth his hand toward his disciples, and said, Behold my mother and my brethren! 50 For whosoever shall do the will of my Father which is in heaven, the same is my brother, and sister, and mother. <div eID="gen22240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22241" type="x-p"/> Many excellent, useful sayings came from the mouth of our Lord Jesus upon particular occasions; even his digressions were instructive, as well as his set discourses: as here, <div eID="gen22241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22242" type="x-p"/> Observe, I. How Christ was interrupted in his preaching by <hi type="italic">his mother and his brethren,</hi> that <hi type="italic">stood without, desiring to speak with him</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.40">v. 40</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.47">47</reference>); which desire of theirs was conveyed to him through the crowd. It is needless to enquire which of his brethren they were that came along with his mother (perhaps they were those <hi type="italic">who did not believe in him,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.7.5">John vii. 5</reference>); or what their business was; perhaps it was only designed to oblige him to break off, for fear he should fatigue himself, or to caution him to take heed of giving offence by his discourse to the Pharisees, and or involving himself in a difficulty; as if they could teach <hi type="italic">him</hi> wisdom. <div eID="gen22242" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22243" type="x-p"/> 1. He was as yet talking to the people. Note, Christ's preaching was talking; it was plain, easy, and familiar, and suited to their capacity and case. What Christ had delivered had been cavilled at, and yet he went on. Note, The opposition we meet within our work, must not drive us from it. He left off talking with the Pharisees, for he saw he could do no good with them; but continued to talk to the common people, who, not having such a conceit of their knowledge as the Pharisees had, were willing to learn. <div eID="gen22243" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22244" type="x-p"/> 2. His mother and brethren stood without, desiring to speak with him, when they should have been standing within, desiring to hear him. They had the advantage of his daily converse in private, and therefore were less mindful to attend upon his public preaching. Note, Frequently those who are nearest to the means of knowledge and grace, are most negligent. Familiarity and easiness of access breed some degree of contempt. We are apt to neglect <hi type="italic">that</hi> this day, which we think we may have any day, for getting that it is only the present time we can be sure of; tomorrow is none of ours. There is too much truth in that common proverb, "The nearer the church, the further from God;" it is pity it should be so. <div eID="gen22244" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22245" type="x-p"/> 3. They not only would not hear him themselves, but they interrupted others that <hi type="italic">heard him gladly.</hi> The devil was a sworn enemy to our Saviour's preaching. He had sought to baffle his discourse by the unreasonable cavils of the scribes and Pharisees, and when he could not gain his point that way, he endeavoured to break it off by the unseasonable visits of relations. Note, We often meet with hindrances and obstructions in our work, by our friends that are about us, and are taken off by civil respects from our spiritual concerns. Those who really wish well to us and to our work, may sometimes, by their indiscretion, prove our back-friends, and impediments to us in our duty; as <hi type="italic">Peter</hi> was offensive to Christ, with his, "<hi type="italic">Master, spare thyself,</hi>" when he thought himself very officious. The mother of our Lord desired to speak with him; it seemed she had not then learned to command her Son, as the iniquity and idolatry of the church of Rome has since pretended to teach her: nor was she so free from fault and folly as they would make her. It was Christ's prerogative, and not his mother's, to do every thing wisely, and well, and in its season. Christ once said to his mother, <hi type="italic">How is it that ye sought me? Wist he not, that I must be about my Father's business?</hi> And it was then said, she <hi type="italic">laid up that saying in her heart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.49">Luke ii. 49</reference>); but if she had remembered it now, she would not have given him this interruption when he was about his Father's business. Note, There is many a good truth that we thought was well laid up when we heard it, which yet is out of the way when we have occasion to use it. <div eID="gen22245" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22246" type="x-p"/> II. How he resented this interruption, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.48-Matt.12.50">v. 48-50</reference>. <div eID="gen22246" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22247" type="x-p"/> 1. He would not hearken to it; he was so intent upon his work, that no natural or civil respects should take him off from it. <hi type="italic">Who is my mother and who are my brethren?</hi> Not that natural affection is to be put off, or that, under pretence of religion, we may be disrespectful to parents, or unkind to other relations; but <hi type="italic">every thing is beautiful in its season,</hi> and the less duty must stand by, while the greater is done. When our regard to our relations comes in competition with the service of God, and the improving of an opportunity to <hi type="italic">do good,</hi> in such a case, we must <hi type="italic">say to our Father, I have not seen him,</hi> as Levi did, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.9">Deut. xxxiii. 9</reference>. The nearest relations must be comparatively hated, that is, we must love them less than Christ (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.26">Luke xiv. 26</reference>), and our duty to God must have the preference. This Christ has here given us an example of; <hi type="italic">the zeal of God's house</hi> did so far <hi type="italic">eat him up,</hi> that it made him not only forget himself, but forget his dearest relations. And we must not take it ill of our friends, nor put it upon the score of their wickedness, if they prefer the pleasing of God before the pleasing of us; but we must readily forgive those neglects which may be easily imputed to a pious zeal for God's glory and others' good. Nay, we must deny ourselves and our own satisfaction, rather than do that which may any way divert our friends from, or distract them in, their duty to God. <div eID="gen22247" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22248" type="x-p"/> 2. He took that occasion to prefer his disciples, who were his spiritual kindred, before his natural relations as such: which was a good reason why he would not leave preaching to speak with his brethren. He would rather be profiting his disciples, than pleasing his relations. Observe, <div eID="gen22248" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22249" type="x-p"/> (1.) The description of Christ's disciples. They are such as <hi type="italic">do the will of his Father;</hi> not only hear it, and know it, and talk of it, but <hi type="italic">do it;</hi> for doing the will of God is the best preparative for discipleship (<reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>), and the best proof of it (<reference osisRef="Matt.7.21">ch. vii. 21</reference>); <hi type="italic">that</hi> denominates us his disciples indeed. Christ does not say, "Whosoever shall do my will," for he came not to seek or do his own will distinct from his Father's: his will and his Father's are the same; but he refers us to his Father's will, because now in his present state and work he referred himself to it, <reference osisRef="John.6.38">John vi. 38</reference>. <div eID="gen22249" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22250" type="x-p"/> (2.) The dignity of Christ's disciples: <hi type="italic">The same is my brother, and sister, and mother.</hi> His disciples, that had left all to follow him, and embraced his doctrine, were dearer to him than any that were akin to him according to the flesh. They had preferred Christ before their relations; they <hi type="italic">left their father</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.22">ch. iv. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.37">x. 37</reference>); and now to make them amends, and to show that there was no love lost, he preferred them before his relations. Did not they hereby receive, in point of honour, <hi type="italic">a hundred fold?</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.19.29">ch. xix. 29</reference>. It was very endearing and very encouraging for Christ to say, <hi type="italic">Behold my mother and my brethren;</hi> yet it was not <hi type="italic">their</hi> privilege alone, <hi type="italic">this honour have all the saints.</hi> Note, All obedient believers are near akin to Jesus Christ. They wear his name, bear his image, have his nature, are of his family. He loves them, converses freely with them as his relations. He bids them welcome to his table, takes care of them, provides for them, sees that they want nothing that is fit for them: when he died he left them rich legacies, now he is in heaven he keeps up a correspondence with them, and will have them all with him at last, and will in nothing fail to <hi type="italic">do the kinsman's part</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ruth.3.13">Ruth iii. 13</reference>), nor will ever be ashamed of his poor relations, but will confess them before men, before the angels, and before his Father.  <chapter eID="Matt.12"/> <div eID="gen22250" type="x-p"/>

entries.94b06781700305329024c274ab30deadc5fc998b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13540"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 12</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.12.1-Matt.12.8">Mt 12:1-8</reference>. Plucking Corn Ears on the Sabbath Day. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.2.23-Mark.2.28">Mr 2:23-28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.1-Luke.6.5">Lu 6:1-5</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The season of the year when this occurred is determined by the event itself. Ripe corn ears are found in the fields only just before harvest. The barley harvest seems clearly intended here, at the close of our March and beginning of our April. It coincided with the Passover season, as the wheat harvest with Pentecost. But in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.1">Lu 6:1</reference>) we have a still more definite note of time, if we could be certain of the meaning of the peculiar term which he employs to express it. "It came to pass (he says) on the sabbath, which was the first-second," for that is the proper rendering of the word, and not "the second sabbath after the first," as in our version. Of the various conjectures what this may mean, that of Scaliger is the most approved, and, as we think, the freest from difficulty, namely, the first sabbath after the second day of the Passover; that is, the first of the seven sabbaths which were to be reckoned from the second day of the Passover, which was itself a sabbath, until the next feast, the feast of Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.15">Le 23:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.16">16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.16.9">De 16:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.16.10">10</reference>) In this case, the day meant by the Evangelist is the first of those seven sabbaths intervening between Passover and Pentecost. And if we are right in regarding the "feast" mentioned in <reference osisRef="John.5.1">Joh 5:1</reference> as a Passover, and consequently the second during our Lord's public ministry (see on <reference osisRef="John.5.1">Joh 5:1</reference>), this plucking of the ears of corn must have occurred immediately after the scene and the discourse recorded in <reference osisRef="John.5.19-John.5.47">Joh 5:19-47</reference>, which, doubtless, would induce our Lord to hasten His departure for the north, to avoid the wrath of the Pharisees, which He had kindled at Jerusalem. Here, accordingly, we find Him in the fields--</hi>on His way probably to Galilee.<div eID="gen25909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25910" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13540"/><hi type="bold">1. At that time Jesus went on the sabbath day through the corn--</hi>"the cornfields" (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.23">Mr 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.1">Lu 6:1</reference>).<div eID="gen25910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25911" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and his disciples were an hungered--</hi>not as one may be before his regular meals; but evidently from shortness of provisions: for Jesus defends their plucking the corn-ears and eating them on the plea of necessity.<div eID="gen25911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and began to pluck the ears of corn, and to eat--</hi>"rubbing them in their hands" (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.1">Lu 6:1</reference>). <div eID="gen25912" type="x-p"/>
entries.787d6e5a6283db481143c08e1fe399b3e8275e4e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13541"/><div sID="gen25913" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13541"/><hi type="bold">2. But when the Pharisees saw it, they said unto him, Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day--</hi>The act itself was expressly permitted (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.25">De 23:25</reference>). But as being "servile work," which was prohibited on the sabbath day, it was regarded as sinful. <div eID="gen25913" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4c998de38f3e3183d805d0444b69c5477745d58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13542"/><div sID="gen25914" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13542"/><hi type="bold">3. But he said unto them, Have ye not read--</hi>or, as Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.25">Mr 2:25</reference>) has it, "Have ye never read."<div eID="gen25914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25915" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what David did when he was an hungered, and they that were with him--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Sam.21.1-1Sam.21.6">1Sa 21:1-6</reference>) <div eID="gen25915" type="x-p"/>
entries.1c0cf51d43fc6f35436542c20e15d2548431bf87: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13543"/><div sID="gen25916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13543"/><hi type="bold">4. How he entered into the house of God, and did eat the showbread, which was not lawful for him to eat, neither for them which were with him, but only for the priests?--</hi>No example could be more apposite than this. The man after God's own heart, of whom the Jews ever boasted, when suffering in God's cause and straitened for provisions, asked and obtained from the high priest what, according to the law, it was illegal for anyone save the priests to touch. Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.26">Mr 2:26</reference>) says this occurred "in the days of Abiathar the high priest." But this means not during his high priesthood--for it was under that of his father Ahimelech--but simply, in his time. Ahimelech was soon succeeded by Abiathar, whose connection with David, and prominence during his reign, may account for his name, rather than his father's, being here introduced. Yet there is not a little confusion in what is said of these priests in different parts of the Old Testament. Thus he is called both the son of the father of Ahimelech (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.20">1Sa 22:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.17">2Sa 8:17</reference>); and Ahimelech is called Ahiah (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.3">1Sa 14:3</reference>), and Abimelech (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.16">1Ch 18:16</reference>). <div eID="gen25916" type="x-p"/>
entries.a8340430c8ce676e7ced628aabdec1af7b94aac6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13544"/><div sID="gen25917" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13544"/><hi type="bold">5. Or have ye not read in the law, how that on the sabbath days the priests in the temple profane the sabbath--</hi>by doing "servile work."<div eID="gen25917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25918" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and are blameless?--</hi>The double offerings required on the sabbath day (<reference osisRef="Num.28.9">Nu 28:9</reference>) could not be presented, and the new-baked showbread (<reference osisRef="Lev.24.5">Le 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.32">1Ch 9:32</reference>) could not be prepared and presented every sabbath morning, without a good deal of servile work on the part of the priests; not to speak of circumcision, which, when the child's eighth day happened to fall on a sabbath, had to be performed by the priests on that day. (See on <reference osisRef="John.7.22">Joh 7:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.7.23">23</reference>). <div eID="gen25918" type="x-p"/>
entries.614774f50b8d7c0806d3cc9653379b4632db4dbc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13545"/><div sID="gen25919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13545"/><hi type="bold">6. But I say unto you, That in this place is one greater than the temple--</hi>or rather, according to the reading which is best supported, "something greater." The argument stands thus: "The ordinary rules for the observance of the sabbath give way before the requirements of the temple; but there are rights here before which the temple itself must give way." Thus indirectly, but not the less decidedly, does our Lord put in His own claims to consideration in this question--claims to be presently put in even more nakedly. <div eID="gen25919" type="x-p"/>
entries.b1cd3484a25bfaa75d4a68a11e34259fb4d4ce8d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13546"/><div sID="gen25920" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13546"/><hi type="bold">7. But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.6.6">Ho 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.6.6-Mic.6.8">Mi 6:6-8</reference>, &c.). See on <reference osisRef="Matt.9.13">Mt 9:13</reference>.<div eID="gen25920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25921" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye would not have condemned the guiltless--</hi>that is, Had ye understood the great principle of all religion, which the Scripture everywhere recognizes--that ceremonial observances must give way before moral duties, and particularly the necessities of nature--ye would have refrained from these captious complaints against men who in this matter are blameless. But our Lord added a specific application of this great principle to the law of the sabbath, preserved only in Mark: "And he said unto them, the sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath" (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.27">Mr 2:27</reference>). A glorious and far-reaching maxim, alike for the permanent establishment of the sabbath and the true freedom of its observance. <div eID="gen25921" type="x-p"/>
entries.ccf6b712c17bfa6e129bc97a2e7e89dd1272c4a1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13547"/><div sID="gen25922" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13547"/><hi type="bold">8. For the Son of man is Lord even of the sabbath day--</hi>In what sense now is the Son of man Lord of the sabbath day? Not surely to abolish it--that surely were a strange lordship, especially just after saying that it was made or instituted for MAN--but to own it, to interpret it, to preside over it, and to ennoble it, by merging it in the "Lord's Day" (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.10">Re 1:10</reference>), breathing into it an air of liberty and love necessarily unknown before, and thus making it the nearest resemblance to the eternal sabbatism.<div eID="gen25922" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.12.9-Matt.12.21">Mt 12:9-21</reference>. The Healing of a Withered Hand on the Sabbath Day and Retirement of Jesus to Avoid Danger. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.3.1-Mark.3.12">Mr 3:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.6-Luke.6.11">Lu 6:6-11</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25923" type="x-p"/> Healing of a Withered Hand (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.9-Matt.12.14">Mt 12:9-14</reference>). <div eID="gen25923" type="x-p"/>
entries.c486abc83698747e04a11b4ea4802f6c6c4ffc92: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13548"/><div sID="gen25924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13548"/><hi type="bold">9. And when he was departed thence--</hi>but "on another sabbath" (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.6">Lu 6:6</reference>).<div eID="gen25924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he went into their synagogue--</hi>"and taught." He had now, no doubt, arrived in Galilee; but this, it would appear, did not occur at Capernaum, for after it was over, He "withdrew Himelf," it is said "to the sea" (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.7">Mr 3:7</reference>), whereas Capernaum was at the sea.<div eID="gen25925" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25926" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">And, behold, there was a man which had his hand withered--</hi>disabled by paralysis (as in <reference osisRef="1Kgs.13.4">1Ki 13:4</reference>). It was his right hand, as Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.6">Lu 6:6</reference>) graphically notes.<div eID="gen25926" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25927" type="x-p"/> And they asked him, saying, Is it lawful to heal on the sabbath days? <hi type="bold">that they might accuse him--</hi>Mark and Luke (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.2">Mr 3:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.7">Lu 6:7</reference>) say they "watched Him whether He would heal on the sabbath day." They were now come to the length of dogging His steps, to collect materials for a charge of impiety against Him. It is probable that it was to their thoughts rather than their words that Jesus addressed Himself in what follows. <div eID="gen25927" type="x-p"/>
entries.308c545027f874f89623e0ac6773e8db72026730: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13549"/><div sID="gen25928" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13549"/>11. And he said unto them, What man shall there be among you that shall have one sheep, and if it fall into a pit on the sabbath day, will he not lay hold on it, and lift it out? <div eID="gen25928" type="x-p"/>
entries.3975cce7b03775307ffdebb4fd961166d899f930: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13550"/><div sID="gen25929" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13550"/><hi type="bold">12. How much then is a man better than a sheep?--</hi>Resistless appeal! "A <hi type="bold">righteous man regardeth the life of his beast" (<reference osisRef="Prov.12.10">Pr 12:10</reference>), and would instinctively rescue it from death or suffering on the sabbath day; how much more his nobler fellow man! But the reasoning, as given in the other two Gospels, is singularly striking: "But He knew their thoughts, and said to the man which had the withered hand, Rise up, and stand forth in the midst. And he arose and stood forth. Then said Jesus unto them, I will ask you one thing: Is it lawful on the sabbath days to do good, or to do evil? to save life or to destroy it?" (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.8">Lu 6:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.6.9">9</reference>), or as in Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.4">Mr 3:4</reference>), "to kill?" He thus shuts them up to this startling alternative: "Not to do good, when it is in the power of our hand to do it, is to do evil; not to save life, when we can, is to kill"--</hi>and must the letter of the sabbath rest be kept at this expense? This unexpected thrust shut their mouths. By this great ethical principle our Lord, we see, held Himself bound, as man. But here we must turn to Mark, whose graphic details make the second Gospel so exceedingly precious. "When He had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, He saith unto the man" (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.5">Mr 3:5</reference>). This is one of the very few passages in the Gospel history which reveal our Lord's feelings. How holy this anger was appears from the "grief" which mingled with it at "the hardness of their hearts." <div eID="gen25929" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f1967be734adecbb11c8fdbc141bfde982c2915: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13551"/><div sID="gen25930" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13551"/><hi type="bold">13. Then saith he to the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it forth--</hi>the power to obey going forth with the word of command.<div eID="gen25930" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25931" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and it was restored whole, like as the other--</hi>The poor man, having faith in this wonderful Healer--which no doubt the whole scene would singularly help to strengthen--disregarded the proud and venomous Pharisees, and thus gloriously put them to shame. <div eID="gen25931" type="x-p"/>
entries.ddc90803a0362008ffd8bcc85df58959f3e1f988: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13552"/><div sID="gen25932" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13552"/><hi type="bold">14. Then the Pharisees went out, and held a council against him, how they might destroy him--</hi>This is the first explicit mention of their murderous designs against our Lord. Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.6.11">Lu 6:11</reference>) says, "they were filled with madness, and communed one with another what they might do to Jesus." But their doubt was not, whether to get rid of Him, but how to compass it. Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.6">Mr 3:6</reference>), as usual, is more definite: "The Pharisees went forth, and straightway took counsel with the Herodians against Him, how they might destroy Him." These Herodians were supporters of Herod's dynasty, created by Cæsar--a political rather than religious party. The Pharisees regarded them as untrue to their religion and country. But here we see them combining together against Christ as a common enemy. So on a subsequent occasion (<reference osisRef="Matt.22.15">Mt 22:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.22.16">16</reference>).<div eID="gen25932" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25933" type="x-p"/> Jesus Retires to Avoid Danger (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.15-Matt.12.21">Mt 12:15-21</reference>). <div eID="gen25933" type="x-p"/>
entries.db317a48939ff9e1ab4d2aa00c8d365962bc5d34: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13553"/><div sID="gen25934" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13553"/><hi type="bold">15. But when Jesus knew it, he withdrew himself from thence--</hi>whither, our Evangelist says not; but Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.7">Mr 3:7</reference>) says "it was to the sea"--to some distance, no doubt, from the scene of the miracle, the madness, and the plotting just recorded.<div eID="gen25934" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25935" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and great multitudes followed him, and he healed them all--</hi>Mark gives the following interesting details: "A great multitude from Galilee followed Him, and from Judea and from Jerusalem, and from Idumea, and from beyond Jordan; and they about Tyre and Sidon, a great multitude, when they had heard what great things He did, came unto Him. And He spake to His disciples, that a small ship"--or "wherry"--"should wait on Him because of the multitude, lest they should throng Him. For He had healed many; insomuch that they pressed upon Him for to touch Him, as many as had plagues. And unclean spirits, when they saw Him, fell down before Him, and cried, saying, Thou art the Son of God. And He straitly charged them that they should not make Him known" (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.7-Mark.3.12">Mr 3:7-12</reference>). How glorious this extorted homage to the Son of God! But as this was not the time, so neither were they the fitting preachers, as Bengel says. (See on <reference osisRef="Mark.1.25">Mr 1:25</reference>, and compare <reference osisRef="Jas.2.19">Jas 2:19</reference>). Coming back now to our Evangelist: after saying, "He healed them all," he continues: <div eID="gen25935" type="x-p"/>
entries.481675a14c9bb3891fc643c7fe686370d2c5e116: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13554"/><div sID="gen25936" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13554"/><hi type="bold">16. And charged them--</hi>the healed.<div eID="gen25936" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25937" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that they should not make him known--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.8.4">Mt 8:4</reference>). <div eID="gen25937" type="x-p"/>
entries.c942f2524762b0e4760763f39ff167ba9fa9060a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13555"/><div sID="gen25938" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13555"/><hi type="bold">17. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>). <div eID="gen25938" type="x-p"/>
entries.9fb5d16917c69bedb7aad9cca02448d0fe0eafea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13556"/><div sID="gen25939" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13556"/>18. Behold my servant, whom I have chosen; my beloved, in whom my soul is well pleased: I will put my Spirit upon him, and he shall show judgment to the Gentiles. <div eID="gen25939" type="x-p"/>
entries.fbbf8309c2d6424704bcfb79bf865bedbb3a9f90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13557"/><div sID="gen25940" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13557"/>19. He shall not strive nor cry; neither shall any man hear his voice in the streets. <div eID="gen25940" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3bd28fc610ae150634ebe41bc5fa68050d8302a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13558"/><div sID="gen25941" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13558"/><hi type="bold">20. A bruised reed shall he not break, and smoking flax shall he not quench, till he send forth judgment unto victory--</hi>"unto truth," says the Hebrew original, and the Septuagint also. But our Evangelist merely seizes the spirit, instead of the letter of the prediction in this point. The grandeur and completeness of Messiah's victories would prove, it seems, not more wonderful than the unobtrusive noiselessness with which they were to be achieved. And whereas one rough touch will break a bruised reed, and quench the flickering, smoking flax, His it should be, with matchless tenderness, love, and skill, to lift up the meek, to strengthen the weak hands and confirm the feeble knees, to comfort all that mourn, to say to them that are of a fearful heart, Be strong, fear not. <div eID="gen25941" type="x-p"/>
entries.522f641c117d8828d4177b68c31e6cda50ca523c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13559"/><div sID="gen25942" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13559"/><hi type="bold">21. And in his name shall the Gentiles trust--</hi>Part of His present audience were Gentiles--from Tyre and Sidon--first-fruits of the great Gentile harvest contemplated in the prophecy.<div eID="gen25942" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.12.22-Matt.12.37">Mt 12:22-37</reference>. A Blind and Dumb Demoniac Healed and Reply to the Malignant Explanation Put upon It. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.3.20-Mark.3.30">Mr 3:20-30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.11.14-Luke.11.23">Lu 11:14-23</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25943" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The precise time of this section is uncertain. Judging from the statements with which Mark introduces it, we should conclude that it was when our Lord's popularity was approaching its zenith, and so before the feeding of the five thousand. But, on the other hand, the advanced state of the charges brought against our Lord, and the plainness of His warnings and denunciations in reply, seem to favor the later period at which Luke introduces it. "And the multitude," says Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.20">Mr 3:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.3.21">21</reference>), "cometh together again," referring back to the immense gathering which Mark had before recorded (<reference osisRef="Mark.2.2">Mr 2:2</reference>)--</hi>"so that they could not so much as eat bread. And when His friends"--or rather, "relatives," as appears from <reference osisRef="Matt.12.31">Mt 12:31</reference>, and see on <reference osisRef="Matt.12.46">Mt 12:46</reference>--"heard of it, they went out to lay hold on Him; for they said, He is beside Himself." Compare <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.13">2Co 5:13</reference>, "For whether we be beside ourselves, it is to God." <div eID="gen25943" type="x-p"/>
entries.59e54438713189b39a359effbe73b1553711a930: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13560"/><div sID="gen25944" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13560"/><hi type="bold">22. Then was brought unto him one possessed with a devil--</hi>"a demonized person."<div eID="gen25944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25945" type="x-p"/> blind and dumb, and he healed him, insomuch that the blind and the dumb both spake and saw. <div eID="gen25945" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f32c3e6ff1fd0f611aaad59f4448252e636dfa0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13561"/><div sID="gen25946" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13561"/><hi type="bold">23. And all the people were amazed, and said, Is not this the son of David?--</hi>The form of the interrogative requires this to be rendered, "Is this the Son of David?" And as questions put in this form (in Greek) suppose doubt, and expect rather a negative answer, the meaning is, "Can it possibly be?"--the people thus indicating their secret impression that this must be He; yet saving themselves from the wrath of the ecclesiastics, which a direct assertion of it would have brought upon them. (On a similar question, see on <reference osisRef="John.4.29">Joh 4:29</reference>; and on the phrase, "Son of David," see on <reference osisRef="Matt.9.27">Mt 9:27</reference>). <div eID="gen25946" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7f1a1d10b05f97d87cbf055a876b9dcaa3b77e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13562"/><div sID="gen25947" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13562"/><hi type="bold">24. But when the Pharisees heard it--</hi>Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.22">Mr 3:22</reference>) says, "the scribes which came down from Jerusalem"; so that this had been a hostile party of the ecclesiastics, who had come all the way from Jerusalem to collect materials for a charge against Him. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.12.14">Mt 12:14</reference>).<div eID="gen25947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25948" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they said, This fellow--</hi>an expression of contempt.<div eID="gen25948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25949" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doth not cast out devils, but by Beelzebub--</hi>rather, "Beelzebul" (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.25">Mt 10:25</reference>).<div eID="gen25949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25950" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the prince of the devils--</hi>Two things are here implied--first, that the bitterest enemies of our Lord were unable to deny the reality of His miracles; and next, that they believed in an organized infernal kingdom of evil, under one chief. This belief would be of small consequence, had not our Lord set His seal to it; but this He immediately does. Stung by the unsophisticated testimony of "all the people," they had no way of holding out against His claims but by the desperate shift of ascribing His miracles to Satan. <div eID="gen25950" type="x-p"/>
entries.3841f58da1e37d208b90667dede26a2b79afcf1b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13563"/><div sID="gen25951" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13563"/><hi type="bold">25. And Jesus knew their thoughts--</hi>"called them" (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.23">Mr 3:23</reference>).<div eID="gen25951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25952" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and said unto them, Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand--</hi>"house," that is, "household" <div eID="gen25952" type="x-p"/>
entries.b29064b14754ca5d7bcab026d14e0fd738281f58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13564"/><div sID="gen25953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13564"/><hi type="bold">26. And if Satan cast out Satan, he is divided against himself; how shall then his kingdom stand?--</hi>The argument here is irresistible. "No organized society can stand--whether kingdom, city, or household--when turned against itself; such intestine war is suicidal: But the works I do are destructive of Satan's kingdom: That I should be in league with Satan, therefore, is incredible and absurd." <div eID="gen25953" type="x-p"/>
entries.95dbf98a388183a5a9b88850dadfd48a8d772284: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13565"/><div sID="gen25954" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13565"/><hi type="bold">27. And if I by Beelzebub cast out devils, by whom do your children--</hi>"your sons," meaning here the "disciples" or pupils of the Pharisees, who were so termed after the familiar language of the Old Testament in speaking of the sons of the prophets (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.35">1Ki 20:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.3">2Ki 2:3</reference>, &c.). Our Lord here seems to admit that such works were wrought by them; in which case the Pharisees stood self-condemned, as expressed in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.19">Lu 11:19</reference>), "Therefore shall they be your judges." <div eID="gen25954" type="x-p"/>
entries.d34a3c29f666e34cb60c6dbbebfd926ca8953a69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13566"/><div sID="gen25955" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13566"/><hi type="bold">28. But if I cast out devils by the Spirit of God--</hi>In Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.20">Lu 11:20</reference>) it is, "with (or 'by') the finger of God." This latter expression is just a figurative way of representing the power of God, while the former tells us the living Personal Agent was made use of by the Lord Jesus in every exercise of that power.<div eID="gen25955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25956" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then--</hi>"no doubt" (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.20">Lu 11:20</reference>).<div eID="gen25956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25957" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the kingdom of God is come unto you--</hi>rather "upon you," as the same expression is rendered in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.20">Lu 11:20</reference>):--that is, "If this expulsion of Satan is, and can be, by no other than the Spirit of God, then is his Destroyer already in the midst of you, and that kingdom which is destined to supplant his is already rising on its ruins." <div eID="gen25957" type="x-p"/>
entries.2c60c13aebe47aef60181b5c284d97f6d7da49f2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13567"/><div sID="gen25958" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13567"/><hi type="bold">29. Or else how can one enter into a strong man's house--</hi>or rather, "the strong man's house."<div eID="gen25958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25959" type="x-p"/> and spoil his goods, except he first bind the strong man? and then he will spoil his house. <div eID="gen25959" type="x-p"/>
entries.f109c3db87cad8178641eb480dbf7b9296f51122: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13568"/><div sID="gen25960" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13568"/><hi type="bold">30. He that is not with me is against me; and he that gathereth not with me scattereth abroad--</hi>On this important parable, in connection with the corresponding one (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.43-Matt.12.45">Mt 12:43-45</reference>), see on <reference osisRef="Luke.11.21-Luke.11.26">Lu 11:21-26</reference>. <div eID="gen25960" type="x-p"/>
entries.0b0757c0de7183f1db0643b32d2ddd73723c77b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13569"/><div sID="gen25961" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13569"/><hi type="bold">31. Wherefore I say unto you, All manner of sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven unto men--</hi>The word "blasphemy" properly signifies "detraction," or "slander." In the New Testament it is applied, as it is here, to vituperation directed against God as well as against men; and in this sense it is to be understood as an aggravated form of sin. Well, says our Lord, all sin--whether in its ordinary or its more aggravated forms--shall find forgiveness with God. Accordingly, in Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.28">Mr 3:28</reference>) the language is still stronger: "All sin shall be forgiven unto the sons of men, and blasphemies wherewith soever they shall blaspheme." There is no sin whatever, it seems, of which it may be said, "That is not a pardonable sin." This glorious assurance is not to be limited by what follows; but, on the contrary, what follows is to be explained by this.<div eID="gen25961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25962" type="x-p"/> but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost shall not be forgiven unto men. <div eID="gen25962" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb8b83571607374b16fb0996598e81a12551009d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13570"/><div sID="gen25963" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13570"/><hi type="bold">32. And whosoever speaketh a word against the Son of man, it shall be forgiven him: but whosoever speaketh against the Holy Ghost, it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world, neither in the world to come--</hi>In Mark the language is awfully strong, "hath never forgiveness, but is in danger of eternal damnation" (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.20">Mr 3:20</reference>)--or rather, according to what appears to be the preferable though very unusual reading, "in danger of eternal guilt"--a guilt which he will underlie for ever. Mark has the important addition (<reference osisRef="Mark.3.30">Mr 3:30</reference>), "Because they said, He hath an unclean spirit." (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.25">Mt 10:25</reference>). What, then, is this sin against the Holy Ghost--the unpardonable sin? One thing is clear: Its unpardonableness cannot arise from anything in the nature of sin itself; for that would be a naked contradiction to the emphatic declaration of <reference osisRef="Matt.12.31">Mt 12:31</reference>, that all manner of sin is pardonable. And what is this but the fundamental truth of the Gospel? (See <reference osisRef="Acts.13.38">Ac 13:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.3.22">Ro 3:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.3.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.1.7">1Jo 1:7</reference>, &c.). Then, again when it is said (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.32">Mt 12:32</reference>), that to speak against or blaspheme the Son of man is pardonable, but the blasphemy against the Holy Ghost is not pardonable, it is not to be conceived that this arises from any greater sanctity in the one blessed Person than the other. These remarks so narrow the question that the true sense of our Lord's words seem to disclose themselves at once. It is a contrast between slandering "the Son of man" in His veiled condition and unfinished work--which might be done "ignorantly, in unbelief" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.13">1Ti 1:13</reference>), and slandering the same blessed Person after the blaze of glory which the Holy Ghost was soon to throw around His claims, and in the full knowledge of all that. This would be to slander Him with eyes open, or to do it "presumptuously." To blaspheme Christ in the former condition--when even the apostles stumbled at many things--left them still open to conviction on fuller light: but to blaspheme Him in the latter condition would be to hate the light the clearer it became, and resolutely to shut it out; which, of course, precludes salvation. (See on <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26-Heb.10.29">He 10:26-29</reference>). The Pharisees had not as yet done this; but in charging Jesus with being in league with hell they were displaying beforehand a malignant determination to shut their eyes to all evidence, and so, bordering upon, and in spirit committing, the unpardonable sin. <div eID="gen25963" type="x-p"/>
entries.891d0a9a2294489654a4fea1844a8e469c7e4fe2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13571"/><div sID="gen25964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13571"/>33. Either make the tree good, &c. <div eID="gen25964" type="x-p"/>
entries.8066e17878481f6e3d25412bf0e71c4599f278b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13572"/><div sID="gen25965" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13572"/><hi type="bold">34. O generation of vipers--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.3.7">Mt 3:7</reference>).<div eID="gen25965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25966" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how can ye, being evil, speak good things? for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh--</hi>a principle obvious enough, yet of deepest significance and vast application. In <reference osisRef="Luke.6.45">Lu 6:45</reference> we find it uttered as part of the discourse delivered after the choice of the apostles. <div eID="gen25966" type="x-p"/>
entries.e40f68c08a418db4ef7537fa9b4e6abe020674e4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13573"/><div sID="gen25967" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13573"/><hi type="bold">35. A good man, out of the good treasure of the heart, bringeth forth good things--</hi>or, "putteth forth good things":<div eID="gen25967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25968" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and an evil man, out of the evil treasure, bringeth forth evil things--</hi>or "putteth forth evil things." The word "putteth" indicates the spontaneity of what comes from the heart; for it is out of the abundance of the heart that the mouth speaketh. We have here a new application of a former saying (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.7.16-Matt.7.20">Mt 7:16-20</reference>). Here, the sentiment is, "There are but two kingdoms, interests, parties--with the proper workings of each: If I promote the one, I cannot belong to the other; but they that set themselves in wilful opposition to the kingdom of light openly proclaim to what other kingdom they belong. As for you, in what ye have now uttered, ye have but revealed the venomous malignity of your hearts." <div eID="gen25968" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ad7b3c8dee40ecd72e3bac106e2b8495764b67b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13574"/><div sID="gen25969" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13574"/><hi type="bold">36. But I say unto you, That every idle word that men shall speak, they shall give account thereof in the day of judgment--</hi>They might say, "It was nothing: we meant no evil; we merely threw out a supposition, as one way of accounting for the miracle we witnessed; if it will not stand, let it go; why make so much of it, and bear down with such severity for it?" Jesus replies, "It was not nothing, and at the great day will not be treated as nothing: Words, as the index of the heart, however idle they may seem, will be taken account of, whether good or bad, in estimating character in the day of judgment."<div eID="gen25969" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.12.38-Matt.12.50">Mt 12:38-50</reference>. A Sign Demanded and the Reply--His Mother and Brethren Seek to Speak with Him, and the Answer. ( = <reference osisRef="Luke.11.16">Lu 11:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.24-Luke.11.36">24-36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.3.31-Mark.3.35">Mr 3:31-35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.19-Luke.8.21">Lu 8:19-21</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen25970" type="x-p"/> A Sign Demanded, and the Reply (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.38-Matt.12.45">Mt 12:38-45</reference>).<div eID="gen25970" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25971" type="x-p"/> The occasion of this section was manifestly the same with that of the preceding. <div eID="gen25971" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ce12d65188c94e7898625158c07ae3d5871465f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13575"/><div sID="gen25972" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13575"/><hi type="bold">38. Then certain of the scribes and of the Pharisees answered, saying, Master--</hi>"Teacher," equivalent to "Rabbi."<div eID="gen25972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25973" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we would see a sign from thee--</hi>"a sign from heaven" (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.16">Lu 11:16</reference>); something of an immediate and decisive nature, to show, not that His miracles were real--that they seemed willing to concede--but that they were from above, not from beneath. These were not the same class with those who charged Him with being in league with Satan (as we see from <reference osisRef="Luke.11.15">Lu 11:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.16">16</reference>); but as the spirit of both was similar, the tone of severe rebuke is continued. <div eID="gen25973" type="x-p"/>
entries.c9a9874eca8cecfca16cf0a890131e002be19972: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13576"/><div sID="gen25974" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13576"/><hi type="bold">39. But he answered and said unto them--</hi>"when the people were gathered thick together" (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.29">Lu 11:29</reference>).<div eID="gen25974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25975" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">an evil and adulterous generation--</hi>This latter expression is best explained by <reference osisRef="Jer.3.20">Jr 3:20</reference>, "Surely as a wife treacherously departeth from her husband, so have ye dealt treacherously with Me, O house of Israel, saith the Lord." For this was the relationship in which He stood to the covenant-people--"I am married unto you" (<reference osisRef="Jer.3.14">Jr 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen25975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25976" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seeketh after a sign--</hi>In the eye of Jesus this class were but the spokesmen of their generation, the exponents of the reigning spirit of unbelief.<div eID="gen25976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25977" type="x-p"/> and there shall no sign be given to it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas. <div eID="gen25977" type="x-p"/>
entries.b14cbeabf527e9053aed8fe3980515eb9e616609: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13577"/><div sID="gen25978" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13577"/><hi type="bold">40. For as Jonas was--</hi>"a sign unto the Ninevites, so shall also the Son of man be to this generation" (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.30">Lu 11:30</reference>). For as Jonas was<div eID="gen25978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25979" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">three days and three nights in the whale's belly--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jonah.1.17">Jon 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen25979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">so shall the Son of man be three days and three nights in the heart of the earth--</hi>This was the second public announcement of His resurrection three days after His death. (For the first, see <reference osisRef="John.2.19">Joh 2:19</reference>). Jonah's case was analogous to this, as being a signal judgment of God; reversed in three days; and followed by a glorious mission to the Gentiles.
